title: Votes on lobbied matters, set against contact and giving
question: When a lobbying client had a stake in a Board vote, did supervisors vote the client’s way more often when the client’s circle had given to them, or when the lobbyist had contacted them?
finding: Across every final Board roll call on disk where a lobbying client’s side can be read (307 files, 3,297 member votes: lobbied land-use matters, other measures a lobbyist cited by number, and contracts, leases and other money files naming a client), members voted the client’s way in 95.5% of 426 votes where the client’s circle had given to them in the two years before, and in 91.5% of 2,871 where it had not: no more than chance would produce once members voting on the same roll call are compared. Only 23 of those 307 roll calls were divided; on them the figures are 78.1% of 32 against 75.3% of 215 (within chance). The client’s side carried on 288 of the 308 sides taken. Clients opposed a measure in 18 cases and saw it defeated in 1; in 16 the measure they opposed passed with no member voting no. In the other 290 cases (a client seeking passage, or taking a side on an appeal) the client’s side lost 3 times. Taken apart: measures cited by file number, 96.3% of 134 against 83.2% of 1,207 (within chance; on their 11 divided roll calls, within chance); money files naming a client, 98.0% of 146 against 98.8% of 1,205 (within chance; on their 9 divided roll calls, within chance); committee votes on the same files, 97.1% of 69 against 91.7% of 567 (within chance; 3 divided, too few votes on each side to test). Members a client’s lobbyist had contacted voted the client’s way in 86.1% of 776 votes against 93.8% of 2,521 for the rest (within chance). Land-use matters alone, the test as first run: 137 land-use matters with a final roll call were lobbied on, and the client’s side can be read for 79 of them (841 member votes). Members voted the client’s way in 94.0% of 184 votes where the client’s circle had given to them in the two years before, and in 93.3% of 657 votes where it had not: no more than chance would produce once members voting on the same matter are compared. On the 5 matters with a divided roll call the figures are 81.8% of 11 against 78.6% of 42 (within chance).
how: Three sets of final Board roll calls are tested, apart and together. (1) Land-use matters: a matter counts as lobbied when a lobbyist’s report gives its file number (or a related file’s), or names its street address in a contact during the two years before the vote. The client’s side is read from the outcome sought: support or oppose for an ordinance or resolution; for an appeal, only wording that says plainly whether the project or the appeal should win. (2) Every other kind of measure a lobbyist cited by its six-digit file number, where a contact dated in the three years up to the vote sought support or approval (the client wants passage) or opposed it (the client wants defeat); appeal files are left to set 1. (3) Contracts, grants, leases and other money files whose title names as the other party a client then paying a lobbyist, matched as in the money-trail screen; that client is taken to want passage, and gifts and grants the City receives are left out. The final vote is the Board’s last roll call on the measure itself, defined once for all of this project’s analyses; a file whose last such action has member votes in neither the vote page nor the minutes is left out, so an earlier reading never stands in for it. The committee rows use every committee roll call on a motion to recommend one of those files; an aye on a “do not pass” recommendation counts as a vote against the measure, and a vote to refer a file without recommendation is left out, because an aye there neither backs the measure nor blocks it. Each supervisor’s aye or no is then marked as with or against that client. “Circle gave” means the client, its officers, the lobbyist, the firm or its staff contributed to that supervisor’s committees in the two years before the vote. “Contacted” means the client’s lobbyist reported a contact with that supervisor about the matter; for a money file, any contact by the client’s lobbyists with that supervisor in the three years before the vote. Chance is measured by shuffling the giving (or the contact) 4,000 times among the supervisors who voted on the same roll call; “expected” is the average number of with-the-client votes among flagged members under that shuffle. The two percentages in a row are raw shares and can differ for a reason the shuffle removes: where a client opposed a measure that passed with no vote against, every member voted against the client, whoever had been given to or contacted. In the combined rows a file counts once, and a land-use matter stays in set 1. A row added from the wider roll calls is tested only when at least five member votes carry the flag and five do not; otherwise it says too few to test. The roll calls come from two tables of the Board’s vote pages. 240 vote pages on 74 files are in both tables, and the two agree member by member on every one; the final vote chosen is the same in both for 64 of the 64 files where both hold one.
limits: Roll calls are on disk for land-use matters, for Board files about money (contracts, grants, leases, loans, settlements with businesses, gifts and grants accepted, appropriations) and for every measure a lobbyist cited by file number, from 2015 to November 2026. Still missing: ordinances and resolutions that no lobbyist cited by number. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 2 files (160358, 160657) are left out wherever a final vote is counted or tested: for their last passage vote the vote page lists no member and the minutes print the action twice with different tallies, so it is not counted as unanimous and no earlier reading stands in for it. 96.0% of the 3,704 final Board roll calls in the wider table had no vote against, and 95.0% of full-Board land-use roll calls had no dissent (the site’s “Votes, appeals and hearings” page), so this test has little power: with everyone voting aye, a member who received money and one who did not vote alike. The divided roll calls are few and are listed one by one in the screen on divided votes. Votes cast on one roll call are not independent of each other, and the same members recur from one roll call to the next, so the number of separate observations is far smaller than the count of member votes. A lobbyist contacts the members most likely to matter, and donors give to members who already agree with them, so even a gap beyond chance would not show that money moved a vote. Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. The side of an appeal is unreadable for most contacts, which say only “support” or “approval”. A position is read from a few typed words by fixed word lists, and a measure can be amended between the contact and the vote, so that a client who backed the first version may not back the last. The other party to a money file is read from its title and matched to a client by name, which can join two different bodies; such a client has usually won a department’s competition before the Board votes. Members marked excused are left out: the word covers absence from the room as well as stepping aside, and the page does not say which. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
